elliot: quick question — I'm chasing a perf regression where the runtime suddenly switches kernels mid-batch on KV-cache hits. suspect sampling bias in our nsys capture. sharing the flags i used, anyone see something dumb?

maya: what's the capture duration + did you bracket steady-state with NVTX? also are you using trace=cuda or sampling?

elliot: i did a short 8s run, not bracketed, flags below. i wanted both kernel timeline + osrt markers so i used trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt and cpu sampling

elliot: ```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --sample=cpu --sample-interval=500us --duration=8s -o /tmp/kv-batch-run
```

sam: short notes: 1) sampling (cpu) won't record every short GPU kernel; it samples CPU stacks, not exact GPU kernel events — use trace=cuda (you already did) for a faithful kernel timeline. 2) an 8s run + no NVTX warmup can bias results if warmup vs steady-state differs. bracket with NVTX push/pop around steady-state. 3) --sample-interval 500us might be too coarse for some bursts.

maya: +1 to sam. If you want exact kernel start/end and correct ordering, run with trace=cuda and sample=none (or drop --sample). sampling is useful for CPU hotpaths, not kernel boundaries. Also increase duration to 30s or do multiple 10s bracketed runs.

elliot: hmm — i relied on the sampling to point at where code switched kernels. the timeline showed memcpy->small kernel->large matmul repeatedly when KV hit rate rose. i'm wondering if osrt trace is causing kernel split, or if our batching heuristics are evicting KV pages and causing recompute kernels. anyone seen osrt-related kernel splitting?

sam: osrt provides OSRT allocator markers; it shouldn't split kernels by itself. kernel splitting often comes from sequence length changes, different launch configs, or runtime choosing a fallback kernel (quantized vs fp16 path). if KV cache eviction forces a re-embedding step you can get an extra kernel. look at kernel names in the CUDA trace (not sampled).

maya: also check correlation with NVTX ranges: make sure you're pushing an NVTX range around each request or batch phase so you can filter timeline by range. bracketed capture looks like:

maya: ```
# instrument code around steady-state
nvtxRangePushA("steady-state");
... run steady traffic ...
nvtxRangePop();

# then capture on CLI
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-end=nvtx --duration=15s -o /tmp/kv-bracket
```

elliot: good call. i didn't have NVTX around the per-batch hot path. i'll rerun with bracketed captures and drop CPU sampling for now. i'll also do a full trace (15-30s) and attach the .qdrep for triage.

perfbot: perfbot: when you attach the .qdrep please include a short note: workload params (batch size, seq len distro, kv hit rate) + hw (A100 80GB, driver, cuda version). that helps map kernel names to config.

sam: one more tip: if you see kernel name morphing (e.g., matmul_kernel -> matmul_kernel_opt2) search the trace for the preceding memcpy/transpose. sometimes a prefix cache invalidation forces a different kernel path.

elliot: thanks all — rerunning now with NVTX brackets + trace=cuda,nvtx + duration=25s. i'll ping with qdrep link when done. :thumbsup:
